p129.lead: Jesus leaves Nazareth and comes to know men: as boatbuilder in Capernaum, observer in Jerusalem, and traveler around the Mediterranean, finishing a human life before he was thirty.

p129.foot.text: Narrated by a secondary midwayer once assigned to the Apostle Andrew

p129.s0.h: Introduction — A Departure Made Hard by Love
p129.s0.b0: Paper 129 covers Jesus’ twenty-seventh through twenty-ninth years, after he had fully and finally stepped out of the management of the Nazareth household. Right up to his baptism he went on contributing to the family finances and taking a keen interest in the spiritual welfare of his brothers and sisters and the happiness of his mother, but he no longer directed the affairs of the home himself.
p129.s0.b2: That is why leaving was not easy for him. He had given himself so fully to his family that he loved them with a great and fervent affection. Over more than four years he let them see, little by little, that a parting was coming, so that the sadness of separation could be borne. Even when we must leave those we love, the passage suggests, the way we leave can be full of care.
p129.s1.h: I. The Twenty-Seventh Year (A.D. 21) — The Boatbuilder of Capernaum
p129.s1.b0: On a rainy Sunday morning in January of A.D. 21, Jesus took unceremonious leave of his family, saying only that he was going to Tiberias and on to other cities about the Sea of Galilee. He was never again a regular member of that household. Finding little of interest in Tiberias, he went on to Capernaum and joined the business of his father’s friend Zebedee, the boatbuilder.
p129.s1.b1: In little more than a year, using greatly improved methods of steaming the boards, he created a new style of boat far safer for sailing the lake, and in less than five years practically every craft on the lake had come from Zebedee’s shop. For tax purposes he registered himself as a “⟦Q 129:1.8⟧skilled craftsman of Capernaum⟦/Q⟧,” and from then to the end of his earth life he was known as a resident of Capernaum.
p129.s1.b2: He lived in Zebedee’s home. Having long worked alone in the world without a father, he greatly enjoyed this time of working with a father-partner. Zebedee’s wife, Salome, a relative of the former high priest Annas, loved him as she loved her own sons, and her four daughters looked on him as an elder brother. He often went down to the caravan station to keep observing how men lived, and he conducted the services more than half the time that year in the new synagogue built by the Roman commander.

p129.s1.b4: The text names a twofold secret behind the ease young people felt with him: he was always interested in what they were doing, and he seldom offered advice unless they asked for it. He talked freely about politics, sociology, science, and philosophy, but he spoke with authoritative finality only when discussing religion—the relation of man to God.
p129.s1.b6: He enjoyed his life in Capernaum, but he missed the children who had played beside the Nazareth carpenter shop. His brother Jude often came over on the Sabbath to hear him in the synagogue, and the more Jude saw of his eldest brother, the more convinced he became that Jesus was a truly great man. In October Jesus went back for Martha’s wedding, but after that he was not in Nazareth again for over two years.
p129.s1.b7: Zebedee’s sons each saw him differently. James was most drawn to him as a teacher and philosopher, John to his religious teaching, while David respected him only as a mechanic. This year Jesus attained new and high levels of conscious contact with his indwelling Thought Adjuster, and it proved to be the last year he lived a settled life in one place.
p129.s1.b9: Now, between his simple but intensely active past and the still more strenuous public ministry to come, there would intervene a few years of extensive travel. Before he could begin his career of teaching and preaching, his training as a man of the realm had to be completed.
p129.s2.h: II. The Twenty-Eighth Year (A.D. 22) — John’s Promise and the Traveler from India
p129.s2.b0: Before leaving Capernaum in March of A.D. 22, Jesus told John Zebedee that he planned to travel widely until his hour should come, and he asked John to send money to the family at Nazareth each month in his stead. John promised to watch over Jesus’ family as he would his own.
p129.s2.b2: John and Zebedee used the funds entrusted to them to buy a little house in Capernaum and hold it in trust, so that Jesus became the owner of a house without having been told about it. In Jerusalem, with a letter of introduction from Salome, he met the former high priest Annas and inspected the academies of the religious teachers, yet he never asked a single question in public. Annas looked on him as a great man, but he knew Jesus would never be granted the status of a regular teacher, since he had not been trained in those schools.
p129.s2.b3: The Nazareth family, knowing nothing of the arrangement with John, decided the time had come to get along without further help from Jesus. James remembered his contract with Jesus and, with his brothers, at once took full responsibility for the family. Years of training had borne their fruit. At Passover the whole Zebedee family came up to Jerusalem and celebrated the feast in Annas’s home as one happy family.
p129.s2.b4: During Passover week Jesus met a wealthy traveler from India and his son. They asked him to come with them to Rome and around the Mediterranean as interpreter and as tutor for the son, and when Jesus raised the needs of his family, the father offered to advance him a year’s wages. Jesus turned that sum over to John and set out on the journey. Only Zebedee knew of it, and he kept the secret to the end.
p129.s2.b5: While he was away the family did well. Jude increased his share and kept it up until he married, and though they needed little help, John took presents each month to Mary and Ruth, as Jesus had instructed. Yet as the journey lengthened, the family all but gave Jesus up for dead; only Zebedee’s assurances kept hope alive in Mary’s heart.
p129.s3.h: III. The Twenty-Ninth Year (A.D. 23) — A Mediterranean Journey to Know Men
p129.s3.b0: The whole of the twenty-ninth year was spent on the tour of the Mediterranean world. Throughout the journey Jesus was known as the Damascus scribe, and on the return trip as the Jewish tutor. His family believed he had been in Alexandria, and he did nothing to change that belief.
p129.s3.b1: To understand such apparently strange conduct, the narrator says, we must keep in mind the motive of the bestowal. Jesus was careful not to build up an overattractive and attention-consuming personal career, or to make overpowering appeals to his fellows. And though he lived on Urantia, he lived his life for his entire universe.
p129.s3.b3: This journey was a phase of his life that he never revealed to his family or to the apostles. Some friends thought he had gone to Damascus, others to India. Yet in that quiet time he practically completed his educational contact-training with the diverse peoples of his day, and he just about learned how man lived and wrought out his existence on Urantia.

p129.s3.b6: By the end of this journey he virtually knew, with all human certainty, that he was a Creator Son. The Adjuster brought up in his mind, little by little, shadowy memories of his Paradise experience; the last of these, his farewell conference with Immanuel, became clear only on the day of his baptism in the Jordan.
p129.s4.h: IV. The Human Jesus — Not a Pattern but a Way
p129.s4.b0: To the onlooking celestial intelligences, this journey was the most enthralling of all his earth experiences up to the cross. He was still the carpenter of Nazareth, the boatbuilder of Capernaum, the scribe of Damascus; the Adjuster had not yet fully mastered his mortal identity. He was still a man among men.
p129.s4.b1: His purely human religious experience well-nigh reached its apex in this year. From the arrival of his Adjuster until the day the material mind and the spirit mind were made one, it was a steady, gradual growth, and its completion came on the day of his baptism. Though he did not appear to spend many seasons in formal prayer, he perfected ever more effective ways of communing with the indwelling spirit presence.
p129.s4.b3: He was also a man acquainted with grief, and he knows the thoughts, feelings, and impulses of mortals from birth to death. He even experienced the higher phases of human and Adjuster reconciliation that so few Urantia mortals ever attain. His life did not win the universal approval of his contemporaries, but it received full and unqualified acceptance by the Universal Father.
p129.s4.b4: The narrator sums up that his life achieved two things at once: the fullness of the revelation of the eternal God to mortal man, and the presentation of a perfected human personality to the satisfaction of the Infinite Creator. Yet, as the table below makes plain, that perfection is not a demand that we copy the same life.

p129.s5.b0: By the end of his twenty-ninth year Jesus had virtually finished living the life required of mortals as sojourners in the flesh. He came as the fullness of God made manifest to man; he had now become well-nigh the perfection of man awaiting the occasion to be manifest to God—and he did it all before he was thirty. The paper shows that this perfection came not through special wonders but through ordinary days of working, learning, and meeting people.

p130.lead: Jesus as the scribe of Damascus: with the Indian merchant Gonod and his son Ganid, from Joppa to Rome, offering words of truth to one person after another along the way.

p130.foot.text: Narrated by a secondary midwayer once assigned to the Apostle Andrew

p130.s0.h: Introduction — On the Road with Gonod and Ganid
p130.s0.b0: With Paper 130 the story of the Mediterranean journey begins. On April 26, A.D. 22, Jesus left Jerusalem with Gonod and his son Ganid, natives of India, and he said good-bye to them in December of the following year at Charax on the Persian Gulf. He spent about half of each day teaching Ganid and interpreting for Gonod, and he gave the rest to close personal contacts with the people he met along the way.

p130.s0.b2: The narrator explains that in recounting these conversations he will freely translate Jesus’ words into the modern phrasing current at the time of this presentation. This paper covers the first half of the journey, up to the arrival in Rome.
p130.s1.h: I. At Joppa — Discourse on Jonah and on Evil
p130.s1.b0: At Joppa Jesus became warm friends with Gadiah, a young Philistine who worked as interpreter for Simon the tanner. When a great truth seeker meets a great truth giver, the narrator says, the result is a liberating enlightenment. Standing at the landing from which Jonah was said to have sailed, Gadiah asked whether Jesus believed the story of the big fish. Jesus saw that the story had impressed on the young man the folly of running away from duty, and he said nothing that would undermine that motivation.
p130.s1.b2: His answer was that flight from duty leads to struggles with the whales of selfishness, but that those who seek God with a heart hungry for truth will be delivered from whatever depths they have fallen into and cast up on the dry land of fresh opportunities for service. At their last meeting Gadiah asked why a good God permits evil. Many still believed then that God creates both good and evil, but Jesus never taught such error.

p130.s1.b4: Gadiah was fully satisfied with the answer. Later he heard Peter preach, became a profound believer in Jesus, and had much to do with Simon the leather merchant’s decision to embrace Christianity. This view of evil, not as God’s work but as the fruit of immature choices, leads the reader to learn better choosing rather than to blame God in the face of suffering.
p130.s2.h: II. At Caesarea — No Man Is a Stranger
p130.s2.b0: While they waited at Caesarea because the ship’s steering paddle was in danger of cleaving, Jesus helped make a new one. At the inn he had long talks with a Taoist merchant from Mongolia, who went home and taught advanced truths about the One God. The narrator takes the occasion to regret that the early church sent no one like Peter or Paul into Asia.
p130.s2.b1: Anaxand, a young Greek in the shipyard, asked why the Gods, if they cared about him, did not remove his cruel foreman. Jesus answered that perhaps the man had been brought near so that Anaxand might lead him into a better way, and he encouraged him that the good in him could overcome the evil in the other. That night Anaxand and his foreman sought Jesus’ advice together.
p130.s2.b4: When Ganid asked why he spent so much time visiting strangers, Jesus replied that no man is a stranger to one who knows God. He also explained that doing God’s will is the progressive experience of partnership with God’s choice and of becoming more and more like him. Watching a shepherd dog, he taught that the dog has a mind and a kind of will, but lacks the power to know God, who is spirit, or to choose eternal values; after that day Ganid gave up his belief in the transmigration of human souls into animals.
p130.s3.h: III. At Alexandria — The Lighthouse and the Library
p130.s3.b0: Before the lighthouse of Pharos, Jesus told Ganid that when he returned to India he should be like that lighthouse to those who sit in darkness, showing them the way to the harbor of salvation, and Ganid said he would. In the library, with its nearly one million manuscripts, the two discussed the religions of the world day after day. Jesus pointed out the truth in each, while always adding that Yahweh was the God developed from the revelations of Melchizedek and the covenant of Abraham.
p130.s3.b1: Under Jesus’ direction Ganid collected the teachings of the world’s religions that recognized a Universal Deity, and he was surprised to find how much the best authors of sacred literature agreed about the eternal God. One day while Jesus was interpreting lectures at the museum, Ganid said he ought to teach the professors themselves, but Jesus smiled and declined.
p130.s3.b3: They hoped to hear Philo, who was trying to harmonize Greek philosophy and Hebrew theology, but he lay sick throughout their stay. Jesus commended much in Greek philosophy and Stoic doctrine to Ganid, yet he impressed on him that such systems were religions only in the sense that they led men to find God and enjoy a living experience in knowing the Eternal.
p130.s4.h: IV. Discourse on Reality — Knowledge, Truth, and Wisdom
p130.s4.b0: On the night before they left Alexandria, after meeting a professor who lectured on Plato, Jesus gave Ganid a long account of universe reality. Material things are the time-space repercussions of the Paradise Pattern and the Universal Mind of God, and the creature becomes one with the Creator only by consistently conforming his will to the Creator’s will. Just as a one-eyed person cannot see depth, neither the material scientist alone nor the spiritual mystic alone can see the true depths of reality.

p130.s4.b3: He also explained evil as a relativity concept. Error is the penalty of imperfection, the shadow of relative incompleteness that must fall across man’s ascending path to Paradise. And he warned that all static, dead concepts are potentially evil: fixed ideas invariably retard science, politics, society, and religion.
p130.s5.h: V–VI. On the Island of Crete; The Young Man Who Was Afraid
p130.s5.b0: In Crete, when Ganid asked why he did not become a public teacher, Jesus replied that only time ripens green fruit and that his tomorrow was wholly in his Father’s hands. At Fair Havens he drew a slave girl away from a drunken man who was attacking her and held the man off with his outstretched arm until he had exhausted himself; Ganid found it hard to understand why Jesus did not strike him.
p130.s5.b2: In the mountains Jesus met Fortune, a young man gripped by fear and a sense of inferiority. First he asked the youth for directions, letting him gladly share what he knew; then he offered in turn to show him the way to the destiny he was seeking in his heart. He reminded him that he had a strong body, a clear mind, and above all an indwelling spirit.

p130.s5.b5: Fortune later became the leader of the Christians in Crete. At Cyrene, Jesus and Ganid gave first aid to a boy named Rufus, injured when an oxcart broke down; his father, Simon, never dreamed that the man whose cross he would one day carry was the stranger who had once befriended his son.
p130.s6.h: VII. At Carthage — Discourse on Time and Space
p130.s6.b0: On the way to Carthage, Gonod and Ganid discovered that Jesus was a good storyteller and that he had been reared in Galilee. When Ganid asked how to make friends, Jesus told him to take a real interest in others, learn to love them, and watch for chances to do something for them.
p130.s6.b2: At Carthage he talked with a Mithraic priest about time and eternity. Time is the stream of temporal events perceived by creature consciousness, and human personality, indwelt by the Father’s spirit, is the only physically related reality that can transcend the material sequence of events. As man ascends, what once appeared as a line of events is seen more and more as a related whole, and the time-space concept increasingly approaches the timeless and spaceless concepts of the Absolutes.
p130.s7.h: VIII. On the Way to Naples and Rome — Encounters of a Single Day
p130.s7.b0: On Malta, Claudus, who had contemplated taking his life, resolved to face life again. At Syracuse the backslidden Jew Ezra poured out his despair at being unable to find God. At Messina they stayed only a day, yet Jesus encouraged a young fruit vendor to learn to feed his soul as well as his body.
p130.s7.b2: In Naples they saw much poverty and gave many alms, and they spread good cheer with smiles to hundreds of men, women, and children. Then, by way of Capua, they traveled the Appian Way toward Rome, the capital of the empire.
p130.s8.b0: Most of the encounters in Paper 130 look brief and accidental. Yet Jesus began with what each person already held—a story about Jonah, a knowledge of mountain trails, a few pieces of fruit—and led them from there to higher thoughts. Several of those he met later became workers for the gospel, without ever knowing who the stranger had been.

p130.s8.b2: The next paper, Paper 131, “The World’s Religions,” examines the collection of teachings about God from the world’s religions that Ganid began in Alexandria and completed in Rome.
p131.lead: The teachings about God that Ganid gathered from the world’s religions in Alexandria and Rome: the common thread of nine traditions from Cynicism to Confucianism, and the “our religion” he learned from Jesus.

p131.foot.text: Narrated by a secondary midwayer once assigned to the Apostle Andrew

p131.s0.h: Introduction — A Young Man’s Record in Ten Parts
p131.s0.b0: Paper 131 is not a story of events but the presentation of a document. During the stay in Alexandria, Ganid spent much of his time, no small sum of his father’s money, and the labor of more than threescore translators gathering what the world’s religions taught about God and his relation to man. He arranged the material in Alexandria and Rome, and the manuscript was preserved in India for hundreds of years after his death.
p131.s0.b1: The narrator makes plain that the monotheistic teachings in this record were largely derived, directly or indirectly, from the missionaries of Machiventa Melchizedek. Going out from Salem, they sought to spread the doctrine of one God—the Most High—to the ends of the earth. This paper should therefore be read not as a full assessment of each religion but as an anthology of the traces of that common teaching surviving in many traditions.

p131.s1.h: I. Cynicism — The Fullest Preservation of the Melchizedek Teaching
p131.s1.b0: The Cynic passages Ganid chose portray God as the Most High of heaven and earth, the perfected circle of eternity, one God who is compassionate and merciful. He is not far away but omnipresent, the record says, and he lives in the heart of the man who fears his holy name.
p131.s1.b2: The record also distinguishes knowledge from wisdom: man gains knowledge from human experience but derives wisdom from contemplating the Most High. The weary soul finds eternal rest in his arms, and there is a promise of justice—what fruit we do not reap from our plantings in this world we shall receive in the next.
p131.s1.b3: It teaches that the one who knows God looks on all men as equal brothers, and that rich and poor are brothers with one Father. It includes the principle that we should not do to others the evil we would not have done to us, and the teaching that prayerful worship shuns evil.
p131.s2.h: II. Judaism — God the Creator and Shepherd
p131.s2.b0: The section on Judaism is the longest in the paper. The passages chosen by Jesus and Ganid celebrate the one God who made the heavens and the earth, the Lord to be loved with all one’s heart, soul, and might, the One who heals the brokenhearted and dwells with the humble in spirit. In turn come the inescapable divine presence, God as shepherd, and the forgiveness that makes scarlet sins as white as snow.
p131.s2.b2: The selection includes many sayings on humility and quietness: pride goes before destruction; he who rules his own spirit is mightier than he who takes a city; those who wait upon the Lord shall renew their strength. At its heart stands the promise, “⟦Q 131:2.6⟧Fear not, for I am with you.⟦/Q⟧”
p131.s2.b3: The selection closes with a promise to those who love the Lord supremely and their neighbors as themselves: they are called sons of the living God and are invited to dwell forever with him in Paradise. Here Ganid must have seen commandment and promise bound together by love alone.
p131.s3.h: III–IV. Buddhism and Hinduism — The Peace of Faith and the God Within
p131.s3.b0: Ganid was shocked to discover how near Buddhism came to being a great and beautiful religion without a personal and universal Deity. The sayings he chose speak of the fearless peace that faith gives, of gladness springing from a pure heart, and of the truth that the greatest warrior is the one who subdues himself. With them stands a sober warning that every act shall receive its reward.
p131.s3.b2: From the Hindu records Ganid gathered passages confessing God as the creator and controller of the universe of universes, the Light of Lights, the lamp of wisdom dwelling within the soul. Prominent are the teaching that to know God releases the soul and cuts the cords of death, and the prayer to be saved from lust, wrath, and avarice.
p131.s3.b4: The Hindu record calls God the Lord of life, the helper of the distressed, the Good Shepherd of the human flocks, and finally confesses him as our father, brother, and friend. It closes that passage with a longing to know this God in our inner being.
p131.s4.h: V–VI. Zoroastrianism and Suduanism (Jainism) — The Lord of Lights and Self-Conquest
p131.s4.b0: Zoroaster was in direct contact with the descendants of the early Melchizedek missionaries, and their doctrine of one God became central to the religion he founded in Persia. Ganid’s record confesses one Supreme God, the Lord of Lights, who is farthest from us and yet nearest because he dwells within our souls. It also teaches that when we confess our wrongs and resolve not to repeat them, forgiveness takes away the bonds of sin.
p131.s4.b2: The prayers of this tradition go on to ask that we be taught how to live this life in the flesh while preparing for the next life of the spirit. The line Ganid chose declares that the religion is right which leads to union with righteousness.
p131.s4.b3: The tradition then known as the Suduanists, and known today as Jainism, was the third group in India to preserve the Melchizedek teaching. Its record teaches that self is man’s invincible foe, appearing as his four greatest passions: anger, pride, deceit, and greed.
p131.s5.h: VII–IX. Shinto, Taoism, and Confucianism — The Heaven of East Asia
p131.s5.b0: The Shinto record was the one world religion Ganid had never heard of. Its sayings tell of a Lord who regards even the prayer of the poorest man, warn that every hair of pride shuts off saving light, and call the worshiper to come with a clean heart free from falsehood and hypocrisy.
p131.s5.b1: The teachings gathered from the founder of Taoism portray a Supreme One who is pure and tranquil and yet powerful. He seeks no credit for his bestowals; he guides without self-assertion and ministers progression without domination. True goodness, the record says, is like water: it blesses everything and seeks the lowest places.
p131.s5.b3: The Taoist record further teaches that the wise man regards all parts from the point of view of the whole, that those who aspire to greatness must learn to humble themselves, and that injury should be recompensed with kindness. Its conclusion is to help one’s fellows without thought of reward.
p131.s5.b4: Confucianism is introduced as the least God-recognizing of the great religions, yet Ganid’s summary speaks of the One God who rules man from on high and of a Heaven that makes no mistakes. It calls benevolence Heaven’s choicest gift to men and teaches that when we find ourselves in the wrong, we should confess our error without hesitation and quickly make amends.
p131.s5.b5: Set side by side, these records show certain teachings recurring across many traditions, though with different wording and emphasis. The table below lists only the common points found within the passages Ganid chose; it does not summarize the full doctrine of any tradition.

p131.s6.b0: After the arduous labor of compiling the world’s religious records, Ganid wrote down separately the belief he had reached through Jesus’ teaching. He called it “our religion.” His confession opens with loving the one Lord with all one’s mind and heart while loving all his children as oneself.
p131.s6.b2: He wrote that we cannot search out God by knowledge, but we can know him in our hearts by personal experience. The greatest change was that he no longer believed only that God is the Father of all his people, but that he is also his own Father. And he came to the conclusion that to rejoice in God’s fatherhood one must also accept the brotherhood of man.
p131.s6.b3: He wrote that when men begin to feel after God, that is evidence that God has already found them. This echoes what Jesus told Ezra at Syracuse in the previous paper. The insight that the very longing for God is a sign that God has come first is a comfort to anyone who feels lost at the beginning of faith.

p131.s7.b0: Paper 131 shows that truth about God was never the monopoly of one people or one scripture. The seed sown by the Melchizedek missionaries grew in its own form in different languages and cultures, and Ganid was surprised to find how much the best authors agreed about the eternal God. At the same time he learned from Jesus the personal experience of knowing as his own Father the God to whom all those teachings pointed.

p131.s7.b2: The next paper, Paper 132, “The Sojourn at Rome,” continues with the people Jesus met in the capital of the world and the teachings he gave them.
p132.lead: The scribe of Damascus before the emperor: six quiet months of ministry in which Jesus met thirty-two religious leaders and more than five hundred Romans.

p132.foot.text: Narrated by a secondary midwayer once assigned to the Apostle Andrew

p132.s0.h: Introduction — Six Months in the Capital of the World
p132.s0.b0: Jesus reached Rome as companion to the Indian merchant Gonod and his son Ganid. On the third day the three of them appeared before the emperor Tiberius. The usually morose emperor was unusually cheerful that day, talked with them at length, and afterward remarked how he envied Jesus’ bearing. While Gonod was busy with business and Ganid kept his regular hours of study, Jesus came to know this city of two million inhabitants, from the forum to the Capitolium and the Palatine hill.
p132.s0.b2: The narrator states plainly the chief reason Jesus consented to this journey: his desire to study and mingle with the people of the Roman Empire, gathered from every country of the Eastern Hemisphere. This paper shows what he did in those six months, in this order: conversations with philosophers, personal ministry, counsel to a rich man, help to neighbors, and trips about Rome.
p132.s1.b0: The most valuable of his experiences in Rome was his contact with the religious leaders of the capital. Before the end of the first week he had sought out and befriended the leaders of the Cynics, the Stoics, and the mystery cults, especially the Mithraic group. Foreseeing that his messengers would soon come to Rome to proclaim the kingdom of heaven, he set about preparing the way for their message to be well received. He chose five Stoics, eleven Cynics, and sixteen mystery-cult leaders—thirty-two in all—and associated with them intimately for almost six months. Thirty of them later became pivotal individuals in establishing Christianity in Rome.
p132.s1.b2: His method was to select the truth in what each person already taught, and then to embellish and illuminate that truth until it crowded out the associated error in a short time. The work was entirely personal: he never met more than three of them at once, and most often he taught them singly. It was possible because these men and women were not bound by tradition. The passage invites us to reconsider our own habit of beginning with someone’s mistakes when we want to change them.

p132.s1.b4: Neither Stephen nor the thirty ever realized that they had once talked with the man whose name became the subject of their teaching. Shortly before his death Paul concluded that the “⟦Q 132:0.10⟧tentmaker of Antioch⟦/Q⟧” was also the “⟦Q 132:0.10⟧scribe of Damascus,⟦/Q⟧” and Peter once surmised that this scribe might have been Jesus but quickly dismissed the idea.
p132.s2.h: I. True Values — To Angamon the Stoic
p132.s2.b0: Jesus had an all-night talk with Angamon, the leader of the Stoics. Its gist was that the standard of true values must be sought in the spiritual world and on the levels of eternal reality. The scientist as such is limited to discovering the relatedness of material facts; the moment he asserts materialism or idealism, he is already doing philosophy.
p132.s2.b2: Scientists and religionists alike are on trial before the bar of human need. Rather than fight each other, they must justify their survival by serving human progress, and any false science or religion must either purify itself or give way to something truer. The teaching prompts us to ask whether the maturity of our minds keeps pace with the speed of our technology.
p132.s3.h: II. Good and Evil — To Mardus the Cynic
p132.s3.b0: Mardus, the leader of the Cynics, talked with Jesus day after day. Jesus told him that good and evil are words symbolizing relative levels of human comprehension of the universe. The lazy may take social usage or religious tradition as their standard of good, but the surviving soul must make a living choice by the standard set by the indwelling spirit.

p132.s3.b3: The possibility of evil is necessary to moral choosing, but its actuality is not. Potential evil serves well enough as a stimulus to decision, and evil becomes real in experience only when a moral mind chooses it. The perfected personality that reaches Paradise no longer casts any shadow of evil.
p132.s4.h: III. Truth and Faith — To Nabon, the Mithraic High Priest
p132.s4.b0: Nabon, high priest of Mithraism, had thought to make a convert of Jesus, but in fact he himself was being prepared to become one of the early converts to the gospel of the kingdom. Jesus taught him that truth cannot be defined with words, only by living.

p132.s4.b2: There is never conflict between true knowledge and truth. Conflict arises between knowledge and human beliefs colored by prejudice or distorted by fear. Out of mental laziness and fear of the unknown, man tends to crystallize science and dogmatize truth.
p132.s4.b4: Faith releases the activities of the divine spark within the mind. Plants and animals survive in time by passing on identical particles to the next generation, but the human soul survives death through identity association with the immortal spark that indwells it. The saying that perfect spiritual self-restraint equals complete freedom lets us see self-control not as bondage but as liberation.
p132.s5.h: IV. Personal Ministry — Opening with Questions, Then Listening
p132.s5.b0: Jesus spent much time getting to know people of every race and class. He had a double purpose: to learn how they reacted to the life they were living, and to say or do something to make that life richer. He usually began conversations by asking questions, and to those he taught the most, he said the least. The overburdened and anxious found relief in unburdening their souls to a sympathetic listener.

p132.s5.b3: In this way he came into affectionate contact with more than five hundred people, and he always regarded these six months as one of the richest periods of his earth life. The only place in Rome he refused to visit was the public baths, because of the sexual promiscuity that prevailed there.
p132.s6.h: V. Counseling the Rich Man — Where Did This Wealth Come From?
p132.s6.b0: A wealthy Stoic citizen introduced by Angamon asked whether he should keep his wealth or give it away. Jesus stressed more than once that his advice was for this man alone and that he must not become a dictator to other rich men; then he urged him first to analyze honestly the sources of his fortune.

p132.s6.b3: At the heart of this counsel lies brotherhood. If we recognize man as our brother and honestly want to do by him as we would have him do by us, the commonplace dictates of justice, honesty, and fairness will guide us through economic problems. The wealthy Roman promised to begin administering all his wealth according to this counsel the very next day.
p132.s7.h: VI. Social Ministry — The Lost Child and the Widow’s Home
p132.s7.b0: The Creator of a universe spent several hours bringing a lost, crying boy back home. Jesus told Ganid that most people are like that child, crying in fear when they are only a short distance from safety. From that day Ganid watched for lost children for the rest of his life.
p132.s7.b2: The two helped a widow raising five children alone, and they even found a position for her eldest son. When Gonod complained good-naturedly that Jesus was making his son a philosopher or philanthropist, Jesus answered that perhaps he could be all four; and when Gonod urged him to write a book, Jesus replied that his mission was to live a life.
p132.s8.h: VII. Trips about Rome — The Orphan Prophet and a New Religion
p132.s8.b0: On the way to the northern Italian lakes, Jesus did not engage a certain pagan in conversation, because the man was not hungry for truth. You cannot reveal God to those who do not seek him, he taught; our real business is so to live that the Father may reveal himself in our lives.
p132.s8.b1: In the mountains of Switzerland, when Gonod asked about Buddha, Jesus acknowledged him as a great man and even a prophet, yet called him an “orphan prophet” who had lost sight of the Father in heaven. His ship of salvation ran aground just outside the harbor because of faulty charts of navigation.

p132.s8.b4: Ganid’s proposal that the two of them make a new religion together was a wondrous scene for the celestial intelligences, for at that very moment they were in fact making a new and everlasting religion—the revelation of God to man in Jesus. When man goes in partnership with God, great things happen.
p132.s9.b0: In Paper 132 Jesus is not a preacher before crowds but a friend who meets people one by one. He did not attack the errors of others but nurtured the truth within them; to philosophers he gave values and truth, to the rich man stewardship, and to a lost child and a widow a helping hand. His work was not to write a book but to live a life.

p133.lead: From Tarentum to Charax: the last journey of Joshua the teacher, who taught mercy and justice, the soul and the mind, and then said good-bye to his friends from India.

p133.foot.text: Narrated by a secondary midwayer once assigned to the Apostle Andrew

p133.s0.h: Introduction — The Scribe Who Left Without Farewells
p133.s0.b0: When Jesus left Rome, he said good-bye to none of his friends. The scribe of Damascus had appeared without announcement and disappeared in the same way. The Stoics, Cynics, and mystery cultists who had known him formed small groups drawn together by their interest in his teachings, and they kept meeting until the first preachers of Christianity arrived in Rome.
p133.s0.b1: The three travelers walked across Italy along the Appian Way to Tarentum. On the road Ganid asked about India’s caste system, and Jesus replied that although human beings differ in many ways, before God all stand on an equal footing.

p133.s1.h: I. Mercy and Justice — The Work of the Individual and of the Group
p133.s1.b0: Near Tarentum a rough youth was brutally attacking a smaller lad. Jesus rescued the boy and held the attacker until the little one had escaped. But when Ganid began to thrash the bully, Jesus promptly stopped him. Ganid asked: if mercy requires rescuing the smaller boy, does not justice demand punishing the offender? Jesus answered as follows.

p133.s1.b3: Asked what he would do if he himself were attacked, Jesus said he would defend himself against a creature lacking moral judgment, but would not punish a fellow man of sonship status in advance and without judgment. He was absolutely assured that the entire universe was friendly to him. The scene invites us to ask whether, when we are angry, we are trying to make ourselves the judge.
p133.s1.b4: Ganid was never fully satisfied, but after hearing how Jacob, the stone mason’s son, had defended Jesus in boyhood, he reached his own conclusion: few would want to attack so kindly a person, and if anyone did, someone would likely rush to help. Jesus would say only that when such a test came, he would abide by the Father’s will. On another occasion he did give the opinion that organized society had every right to use force in executing its just mandates.
p133.s2.h: II. Embarking at Tarentum — Husband and Wife
p133.s2.b0: At the landing a man was mistreating his wife. Jesus did not rebuke him, but tapped him gently on the shoulder and asked to speak with him privately. He first acknowledged the man’s sense of justice and then asked what had happened. It was not so much his words as his kindly look and sympathetic smile that touched the man’s heart, and he regretted his lack of self-control.
p133.s2.b2: Jesus said that men and women are partners with God, since they cooperate to create beings with the potential of immortal souls. Hearing this, Gonod resolved to reorganize his home when he returned to India.
p133.s2.b3: What stands out here is Jesus’ approach. He stopped the violence without shaming the man in public. He drew him aside, called out the good in him first, and gave him the chance to name his own fault. As a result the man promised to live up to his former pledge, and the couple stood in a tearful embrace. On the boat to Nicopolis, Ganid began speaking with the ship’s steward about religion, and when he got into deep water he called on Joshua for help. The spirit of personal ministry was taking hold of him.
p133.s3.h: III–IV. At Corinth; Personal Work in Corinth — Courtesans and People of Many Trades
p133.s3.b0: In Corinth Jesus held more than twenty sessions with Crispus, the chief ruler of the synagogue, while Ganid observed Jewish family life in his home. Years later, when Paul was driven out of the synagogue, Crispus and his entire family embraced the new religion. Of Aquila and Priscilla, who welcomed Paul, Aquila was one of the Cynics Jesus had met in Rome.
p133.s3.b1: One evening two public women accosted them, and Ganid spoke sharply and rudely motioned them away. Jesus stopped him and asked whether he knew the circumstances that had led them to this way of making a living.
p133.s3.b3: Jesus saw in their faces not wickedness but sorrow, and Ganid apologized. He took the two women to the home of Justus and entrusted them to his wife, Martha, to plan a new life with them. The elder died soon afterward with bright hopes of survival, and the younger became a lifelong member of the first Christian church in Corinth. Asking about someone’s circumstances before condemning them is what lifts people up.

p133.s3.b6: More than half of the people with whom they had intimate conversations during those two months in Corinth later became members of the Christian community. Paul had not intended a long stay in Corinth, but without knowing how well the Jewish tutor had prepared the way, he remained eighteen months. These brief conversations were fitted exactly to each person’s trade and situation. The truth was one, but the words that carried it were translated into the language of each listener’s life.
p133.s4.h: V. At Athens — Discourse on Science
p133.s4.b0: At their inn in Athens, after a Greek philosopher had lectured for almost three hours, Jesus spoke of the place and limits of science. Science can measure energy manifestations but cannot tell what they are. Logic and mathematics are valid in the material world, but they should not be regarded as infallible when applied to the problems of life.

p133.s4.b2: If one man can shear a sheep in ten minutes, ten men cannot shear it in one minute. Yet a group of people working in coordinated harmony stands for a force far greater than the simple sum of its parts. It is an everyday lesson that the worth of people working together cannot be reckoned by arithmetic alone.
p133.s5.h: VI–VII. At Ephesus; The Sojourn at Cyprus — Discourses on the Soul and on Mind
p133.s5.b0: At Ephesus a Greek thinker asked what Jesus meant by “soul.” Jesus described it as the self-reflective, truth-discerning part of man that elevates him above the animal level. Self-consciousness alone is not the soul; moral self-consciousness is its foundation. The divine spirit arrives with the mind’s first moral activity, and that is the occasion of the birth of the soul.
p133.s5.b2: Jesus explained that the saving or losing of a soul depends on whether the moral consciousness attains survival status through eternal alliance with the immortal spirit. All soul conflict arises from a lack of harmony between the moral, or spiritual, self-consciousness and the purely intellectual self-consciousness. The soul cannot be proved by material science or by pure spirit-testing, yet every morally conscious mortal knows of its existence as a real personal experience.
p133.s5.b3: In the mountains of Cyprus Ganid fell gravely ill with fever, and Jesus nursed him with skill and tenderness. During his recovery Jesus taught about the human mind. Ideas are sensations plus the reflective interpretation of the self, and the self is more than the sum of its sensations. And the mind does not well stand the conflict of double allegiance.
p133.s5.b5: Peace of mind is not won by compromising ideals but by the stalwart assertion of the triumph of what is true, overcoming evil with the force of good. The teaching suggests that clearly choosing a side, rather than folding up our conscience to avoid conflict, is the real road to peace.
p133.s6.h: VIII–IX. At Antioch; In Mesopotamia — The Farewell of Joshua the Teacher
p133.s6.b0: In Antioch Jesus became quieter and more reflective. Ganid sought out a disgruntled Indian employee who was about to be dismissed, told him of the Father in heaven, and helped him with a Hebrew proverb: whatever your hand finds to do, do it with all your might. The pupil had begun to practice what he had learned.
p133.s6.b1: After crossing the desert and reaching Ur, the day of parting finally came. Ganid said that the Father in heaven must be something like his teacher. Jesus saw them off at Charax, and in this world they never learned that Jesus of Nazareth was their teacher Joshua.
p133.s6.b2: At Ur Ganid had a long talk about the difference between knowledge, wisdom, and truth, and he was charmed by the Hebrew wise man’s saying that wisdom, if embraced, will bring one to honor. Gonod and Ganid extended their stay three weeks in hope of persuading Jesus to come with them to India, but his path lay in Palestine.
p133.s7.b0: Paper 133 closes the chapter of Joshua the teacher. On this journey Jesus offered truth suited to the moment to people he met by the roadside, at the landing, and in the inn. He asked about circumstances instead of condemning, showed mercy instead of punishing, and even when speaking of science, the soul, and the mind, pointed to a unified life given to doing God’s will.

p134.s0.h: Introduction — Choosing Palestine as the Stage
p134.s0.b0: Having closely studied people and nations on the Mediterranean journey, Jesus reached his final decision about the rest of his life. He reconsidered and finally approved the plan by which he had been born of Jewish parents in Palestine, and he resolved to finish his mortal career in the very land where he had entered human experience as a helpless babe.

p134.s1.h: I. The Thirtieth Year (A.D. 24) — Settling the Family and Departing
p134.s1.b0: Returning by way of Babylon and Damascus, Jesus turned over the little house in Capernaum to his brother James. His family believed he had spent the time studying in Alexandria, and he neither confirmed nor denied it. In Nazareth he had his first long talks with Ruth, the youngest, now nearly fifteen.
p134.s1.b1: Simon and Jude had waited for their eldest brother’s blessing and were married at a double wedding. Then Jesus volunteered to take the place of a caravan conductor who had fallen ill, on a trip lasting a year, and arranged for his mother and Ruth to move into the house in Capernaum. Mary lived there for the rest of her life.
p134.s1.b3: This year great progress was made in the working harmony between his human mind and the indwelling Thought Adjuster. The Adjuster was reorganizing his thinking and rehearsing his mind for the great events ahead.
p134.s2.h: II. The Caravan Trip to the Caspian
p134.s2.b0: The caravan went from Jerusalem by way of Damascus and Lake Urmia, through Assyria, Media, and Parthia, to the southeastern Caspian region. As its executive, Jesus was responsible for the goods and for the safe conduct of the travelers, and he discharged these duties faithfully and wisely. Scores of people along the route were made better by meeting this extraordinary conductor.
p134.s2.b1: This trip carried Jesus nearest to the Orient. He made intimate contact with every surviving race of Urantia except the red, and Europeans and Asiatics alike listened to his words of hope and eternal life. After his return he made Capernaum his home, though he never again lived with his family; he stayed with the Zebedees.
p134.s3.h: III. The Urmia Lectures — A Temple of the Philosophy of Religion
p134.s3.b0: On an island in Lake Urmia stood a lecture amphitheater dedicated to the “⟦Q 134:3.1⟧spirit of religion⟦/Q⟧,” built by the merchant Cymboyton and his three sons. About seventy-five teachers from more than thirty religions lectured and debated there. Only one doctrine was required for a seat on the faculty: each teacher must represent a religion that recognized God—some sort of supreme Deity.
p134.s3.b1: Any teacher who showed intolerance or a contentious spirit was dismissed at once. As an independent teacher, Jesus stayed two weeks on his return and gave twenty-four lectures on “⟦Q 134:3.4⟧The Brotherhood of Men,⟦/Q⟧” with twelve evening sessions of discussion. This was the most systematic and formal of all his teaching on Urantia.
p134.s3.b2: Here the narrator discloses an unusual circumstance. The seraphim of the churches and the seraphim of progress disagreed about including these teachings in the revelation, and in the end the Melchizedek chairman appointed three secondary midwayers to restate Jesus’ teaching for twentieth-century conditions. The sections that follow are therefore not Jesus’ exact words but a statement of his teaching as applied to the modern world.
p134.s4.b0: The brotherhood of men rests on the fatherhood of God, and the kingdom of heaven is a spiritual relationship between God and man. Religions can remain at peace so long as they recognize the spirit sovereignty of God the Father. Intolerance and persecution begin when one religion claims exclusive authority over all others.
p134.s4.b2: The kingdom of heaven creates unity, not uniformity. Spiritually all men are equal, and in it there are no castes or classes. Yet the concept of equality brings peace only when all mutually recognize some supersovereignty above themselves. The Urmia teachers lived in peace because they acknowledged God spiritually and Cymboyton’s authority socially.
p134.s5.h: V. Political Sovereignty — War Is a Symptom
p134.s5.b0: The midwayers state in advance that in their presentation on political sovereignty they have departed more widely from the substance of the Urmia teaching. In Jesus’ day there were only two great world powers, whereas the twentieth century is a peculiarly critical stage in the evolution of political sovereignty.
p134.s5.b2: On an inhabited world there are only two levels of relative sovereignty: the spiritual free will of the individual and the collective sovereignty of mankind as a whole. Every grouping in between has value only so far as it enhances the welfare and progress of man and mankind. The rule of the Most Highs is not for any chosen people but for the greatest good of the greatest number for the greatest length of time.

p134.s5.b4: As sovereignty passes to larger groups, minor wars decrease but the potential for greater wars increases. The obstacle at every stage is the loyalty already mobilized: the loyalty that makes the tribe possible makes the nation difficult, and the patriotism that makes the nation possible complicates the government of mankind. A league of nations can prevent minor wars, but not world wars among the great powers.
p134.s5.b6: The text points to the forty-eight American states, which no longer war among themselves since surrendering their sovereignty and self-determination to the federal government. Just as little Rhode Island has as many senators as great Texas, in a world state the small nations will be as powerful as the great.
p134.s6.b0: If one man is to be absolutely free, another must become an absolute slave. Freedom is therefore relative, possible only under laws that secure the same degree of freedom for all. Religion makes brotherhood spiritually possible, but mankind government is needed to regulate the social, economic, and political problems connected with it.

p134.s6.b3: Under world government the nations do not lose sovereignty but create, for the first time, a real one, and individuals actually enjoy more liberty. The end of the Urmia story, however, is bitter. After Cymboyton’s death, the Christian teachers sent by Abner sought to make their religion dominant over the other beliefs, and five years later the school closed. A faith that had lost its tolerance undid the very teaching it had received.
p134.s7.h: VII. The Thirty-First Year (A.D. 25) — Last Journeys as a Private Individual
p134.s7.b0: Jesus knew that his world travels were about finished. He lived for over two months in Antioch, working three weeks as a tentmaker, then went down the coast through Caesarea, Joppa, and Gaza to Beersheba. From Beersheba to Dan he made his final tour through the heart of Palestine as a private individual. At Bethlehem he saw his birthplace.

p134.s8.h: VIII. The Sojourn on Mount Hermon — Winning the Sovereignty of His Universe
p134.s8.b0: In mid-August of A.D. 25 Jesus left his supplies with a lad named Tiglath and climbed the lonely slopes of Mount Hermon. He asked his Father to send his guardian seraphim back to be with Tiglath, and he went into his last struggle alone, with only his indwelling Thought Adjuster. The beings he wrestled with on the mountain were not phantasms of a starving mind but real beings, his archenemies in the system of Satania.
p134.s8.b1: During this time he finished the mortal task of achieving the circles of mind-understanding and personality-control. In the last week he asked to meet Satan and Caligastia as Joshua ben Joseph. This temptation had nothing to do with food or temple pinnacles; it concerned the sovereignty of a universe.
p134.s8.b3: To every compromise and makeshift, Jesus made only this one reply. On an afternoon in late summer, Michael of Nebadon won the unquestioned sovereignty of his universe, and the Lucifer rebellion and Caligastia secession were virtually settled. The so-called “great temptation” therefore took place before his baptism, not after it. The lesson of the scene is to hold to the single standard of the Father’s will rather than argue at length with temptation.
p134.s9.h: IX. The Time of Waiting — Until the Hour Comes
p134.s9.b0: Coming down from the mountain, Jesus said, “⟦Q 134:8.10⟧I must return to my Father’s business⟦/Q⟧,” and he was a much changed man. At the day of atonement services in Jerusalem he saw the ritual as a misrepresentation of his Father’s character, but his faithful Monitor reminded him that his hour had not yet come. During the feast of tabernacles he left John behind and withdrew alone to the hills.
p134.s9.b2: Back in Capernaum he put on his apron and worked for several months beside James on the interior finishing of large boats. He wasted little time on trifles but was painstaking about the essentials. Even as reports of John the Baptist reached him, he kept working, until in January of A.D. 26, when John had come near Pella, he laid down his tools and declared, “⟦Q 134:9.8⟧My hour has come⟦/Q⟧.” He filled even the waiting before his great mission with faithful labor.
p134.s10.b0: Paper 134 is the bridge from the private Jesus to the public Jesus. He fulfilled his responsibilities as a caravan conductor, taught at Urmia the sole sovereignty of God and the brotherhood of men, and on Mount Hermon, choosing the Father’s will alone, won the sovereignty of his universe. Because that long transformation of mind and spirit was complete, few of those he had once helped ever recognized him when he became a public teacher.

p135.lead: Born a child of promise and raised a lifelong Nazarite shepherd: the life of John the Baptist, last of the old prophets, who proclaimed that the kingdom was at hand.

p135.foot.text: Narrated by a secondary midwayer once assigned to the Apostle Andrew

p135.s0.h: Introduction — A Child of Promise Who Grew Up Ordinary
p135.s0.b0: John the Baptist was born on March 25, 7 B.C., in fulfillment of the promise Gabriel had made to Elizabeth. The narrator makes clear that apart from Gabriel’s visit and Zacharias’s dream, nothing unusual or supernatural attended his birth. He grew up as an ordinary child in a small village west of Jerusalem.
p135.s0.b2: The most eventful occurrence of his early childhood was a visit to Jesus and the Nazareth family when he was a little over six. There was no synagogue school in the village, but Zacharias, a priest, and Elizabeth, herself of priestly descent, gave much time to the mental and spiritual training of their only son.

p135.s1.h: I–II. John Becomes a Nazarite; The Death of Zacharias
p135.s1.b0: At fourteen John was inducted for life into the Nazarite brotherhood at Engedi, by the Dead Sea, vowing to abstain from intoxicating drink, to let his hair grow, and to refrain from touching the dead. A life Nazarite was held in great respect, since such Nazarites were the only persons besides high priests ever permitted to enter the holy of holies. At sixteen, impressed by reading about Elijah, he decided to adopt the prophet’s style of dress.
p135.s1.b1: When his father died, eighteen-year-old John was greatly embarrassed by his vow against contact with the dead, and after the burial he offered the sacrifices required for his cleansing. Visiting Nazareth that year, he had all but resolved to launch out on his lifework, but Jesus’ words and example counseled him to go home and care for his mother.
p135.s1.b3: Because John refused the priest’s allowance, the family’s circumstances grew hard, and he and his mother moved to Hebron, where he kept sheep in the wilderness of Judea. He was so different from most Nazarites that he could not fully fraternize with the brotherhood, though he was very fond of Abner, the leader at Engedi. His waiting—sensing a calling while still caring first for the family before him—shows how to govern an impatient zeal.
p135.s2.h: III. The Life of a Shepherd — A Man of the Wilderness Reading Daniel
p135.s2.b0: Along a brook John built a dozen stone shelters and night corrals, and with Ezda, an orphan lad he had in a way adopted, he lived simply on mutton, goat’s milk, wild honey, and locusts. A shepherd’s life gave him a great deal of time for thought.
p135.s2.b1: He read Daniel’s description of the great image a thousand times and believed that after the kingdoms from Babylon to Rome, the God of heaven would set up a kingdom never to be destroyed. Yet Daniel’s “⟦Q 135:3.3⟧one like the Son of Man⟦/Q⟧” did not harmonize with what his parents had told him about Jesus, and he never completely rose above this confusion. Reports of the wickedness of Rome and Herod convinced him that the end of the age was impending.
p135.s3.h: IV. The Death of Elizabeth — Waiting for Elijah
p135.s3.b0: When his mother died in A.D. 22, John gave his flocks to the brotherhood and fasted and prayed. He knew only the old methods of approach to divinity, and Elijah was his ideal of a prophet. During two and a half years at Engedi he persuaded most of the brotherhood that the end of the age was at hand, though his early teaching rested on the current Jewish idea of the Messiah as a deliverer from gentile rule.
p135.s3.b1: What held him back was Malachi’s promise that Elijah would come first. He knew he was not Elijah, and his doubts kept him from ever calling himself by that name. But Elijah’s influence led him to adopt a direct and blunt assault on the sins and vices of his day.
p135.s4.h: V. The Kingdom of God — The Expectations John Met
p135.s4.b0: To understand John’s message we must know the situation of the Jews. For almost a hundred years Israel had been unable to explain why God’s chosen people remained subject to gentile overlords. The apocalyptists who arose then taught that this suffering was punishment for the nation’s sins and was nearly over, and they equated the end of Roman rule with the end of the age.

p135.s4.b2: In that day “Messiah” meant not one who taught God’s will but one who would actually establish the kingdom of God; a holy man who taught righteous living was called a prophet. So when John cried that the kingdom of heaven was at hand, his hearers took his words in no fewer than half a dozen different senses. That the same words can sound wholly different according to the listener’s expectations is true of the language of faith today as well.
p135.s5.h: VI–VII. John Begins to Preach; John Journeys North — The Cry at the Jordan
p135.s5.b0: In March of A.D. 25 John took his stand by the ancient ford where Joshua had crossed and began to preach to those passing by. A herdsman like Amos and dressed like Elijah, he was taken for a prophet. What was new was that he baptized Jews themselves “⟦Q 135:6.4⟧for the remission of sins.⟦/Q⟧” Baptism had been used for gentile proselytes, but never had Jews been asked to submit to the baptism of repentance.
p135.s5.b1: He was a heroic but tactless preacher, warning the Pharisees and Sadducees who came for baptism to bring forth fruit worthy of repentance. Yet to his disciples he taught the concrete details of a new life.

p135.s5.b3: Traveling north along the Jordan, he spoke for the first time of “⟦Q 135:7.2⟧another one who is to come after me⟦/Q⟧.” The longer he preached, the more confused he grew about the nature of the kingdom, but his conviction that it was coming at once never wavered. In fifteen months he baptized considerably over one hundred thousand penitents.
p135.s5.b5: As his disciples asked questions, John kept adding more helpful and comforting teaching to his early message, “⟦Q 135:7.3⟧Repent and be baptized.⟦/Q⟧” Throngs came from Galilee and the Decapolis, and scores of earnest believers stayed with him day after day. By the time he reached Pella, Jesus had spoken favorably of his message, and James and John, the sons of Zebedee, went down to be baptized and brought Jesus firsthand reports.
p135.s6.h: VIII–IX. Meeting of Jesus and John; Forty Days of Preaching
p135.s6.b0: On January 13, A.D. 26, Jesus laid down his tools in the shop, said, “⟦Q 135:8.3⟧My hour has come⟦/Q⟧,” and set out for Pella with his brothers James and Jude. He took his place in the line of penitents until he stood before John. When John protested that he needed to be baptized by Jesus, Jesus whispered that it was fitting to set this example for his brothers and to let the people know his hour had come.
p135.s6.b2: After the baptism the four men still in the water heard this voice, and Jesus left in silence for the hills to the east, unseen for forty days. Meanwhile John’s camp argued over whether the Messiah would be a military leader or the founder of a spiritual kingdom, and selfish ambitions began to appear. John forbade the disciples who wanted to go in search of Jesus.
p135.s6.b4: When Jesus returned on February 23, John stood on a rock and proclaimed him the Son of God, the deliverer of the world. The next day Jesus left for Galilee, saying only that the Father would guide John in the future as in the past, and the two never again met in the flesh.
p135.s7.h: X–XII. John Journeys South; John in Prison; Death of John the Baptist
p135.s7.b0: After Jesus’ baptism John felt that the responsibility for the coming kingdom was no longer on his shoulders, and he was disconsolate and lonely. Still he kept preaching, increasingly proclaiming mercy to the common people while denouncing corrupt rulers with renewed vehemence. His attack on Herod Antipas’s unlawful marriage, and Herod’s fear of rebellion, led to his arrest on June 12, A.D. 26.
p135.s7.b1: In the prison at Machaerus he was often tempted to doubt why the Messiah did nothing to deliver him. Yet to disciples who resented Jesus’ prosperity he gave a remarkable answer.
p135.s7.b4: Jesus loved John greatly, but knowing that his work on earth was finished and what great things awaited him, he did not interfere in the natural outworking of his career. A few days before John’s death, Jesus answered his message by saying that he would be abundantly blessed in the age to come if he found no occasion to doubt and stumble over him; this word steadied John’s faith.
p135.s7.b5: Herod feared that releasing John would bring rebellion and that killing him would set off a riot among the Pereans who held him a prophet, so he simply kept him in prison. John would never agree to give up public activity as a condition of release. Herod talked with him several times about the kingdom of heaven and was at times impressed, but fear kept him from acting, and at last, at his birthday feast, drawn by Herodias’s scheme and his own drunken oath, he had John beheaded. John’s disciples laid the body in a tomb and went and told Jesus.
p135.s8.b0: The John of Paper 135 was faithful without complete understanding. He never clearly grasped the nature of the kingdom or Jesus’ part in it, and in prison he went through bitter doubt. Yet he finished the work of preparing the way that had been given him, and he knew how to rejoice as one greater than himself increased.

The narrator draws the difference between the two men clearly: John was an eager and earnest worker, while Jesus was a calm and happy laborer. John preached the kingdom of heaven but hardly entered into its happiness.

p136.s1.h: I. Concepts of the Expected Messiah
p136.s1.b0: The Jews saw their history as running from Abraham to the new age of the Messiah. Their titles for the deliverer evolved from “⟦Q 136:1.1⟧the servant of the Lord⟦/Q⟧” to “⟦Q 136:1.1⟧the son of David,⟦/Q⟧” “⟦Q 136:1.1⟧the Son of Man,⟦/Q⟧” and “⟦Q 136:1.6⟧the Son of God⟦/Q⟧.” The rabbis had gathered almost five hundred passages said to foretell the Messiah, yet amid all those details they almost completely lost sight of his personality. They looked for Israel’s temporal exaltation rather than the salvation of the world.
p136.s1.b1: They believed the Messiah would restore the Shekinah, the symbol of the Divine Presence no longer seen in the temple. On the evil nature of man they disagreed: some held that Adam’s sin had cursed the race, others that God had put both good and evil natures into man. Most believed the Messiah delayed because of the nation’s sins, which is why John’s call to repentance had such a powerful appeal.
p136.s1.b2: Above all, they lacked the idea of the human and the divine united in one personality. They imagined the Messiah as a perfected human, as superhuman, even as divine, but never as the union of the two. This became the great stumbling block of Jesus’ early disciples as well.
p136.s2.h: II. The Baptism of Jesus — The Personalization of the Adjuster
p136.s2.b0: Many devout Jews of that time were baptized not for their own sins but for the good of Israel. Jesus’ baptism, too, was in no sense a rite of repentance or for the remission of sins. He was simply following the example of many pious Israelites.
p136.s2.b1: When Jesus went down into the Jordan, he was a mortal who had reached the pinnacle of human evolutionary ascension in the conquest of mind and self-identification with the spirit. Superhuman observers expected to witness the fusion of his Adjuster with his mind, but something new and even greater took place. As John laid his hands on him, the Adjuster took leave of the perfected human soul of Joshua ben Joseph, and in a few moments returned as a Personalized Adjuster.

p136.s2.b4: This day ended the purely human life of Jesus. From then on the Personalized Adjuster was with him throughout his earth life. The narrator also corrects the chronology: counting Tiberius’s years as coemperor, the fifteenth year of his reign was A.D. 26, the year of Jesus’ baptism. Our own baptism or confession of dedication can likewise be more than a rite of cleansing—a decision to do the Father’s will.
p136.s3.h: III. The Forty Days — Told That His Sovereignty Was Complete
p136.s3.b0: Jesus had already overcome the great temptation on Mount Hermon before his baptism. The forty days of retirement afterward were not for fasting or afflicting the soul; he was no ascetic, and he came to destroy such notions. He withdrew to the Perean hills to adjust to his changed relationship with the universe brought about by the personalization of his Adjuster, and to plan his public work.
p136.s3.b1: In the hills he met Gabriel, and then the Constellation Father of Edentia appeared to declare that his sovereignty was complete and to bring him the bestowal release of Immanuel. He was now free to end the bestowal whenever he chose.
p136.s3.b3: According to Gabriel, two things had already been accomplished. The completion of his bestowal in mortal flesh had been demonstrated by the personalization of his Adjuster on the day of his baptism, and the end of the Lucifer rebellion had become a fact of history on the day he came down from Mount Hermon to join the lad Tiglath. The rest of his earth life, then, was not for winning sovereignty but was work he freely chose: the revelation of the Father. During this time James and John, the sons of Zebedee, often came near his shelter but never found him.
p136.s4.h: IV. Plans for Public Work — A Season of Decision, Not Temptation
p136.s4.b0: Jesus first decided not to teach at the same time as John, until John’s work was finished or cut short. Recalling Immanuel’s instructions to leave no permanent writing, he never again wrote on anything except sand. He did not fast during the forty days; on the third day he went in search of food. Nor was he tempted by any evil spirits or rebel beings.
p136.s4.b1: Gabriel reminded him that there were two ways he might manifest himself. On the third day he promised himself to return to the world and finish his earth career, always choosing the Father’s will. From then on the mind of man became the mind of God, though the human selfhood remained, and that mind ever said, “⟦Q 136:4.4⟧Not my will but yours be done.⟦/Q⟧”
p136.s4.b2: He lived in an ancient rock cavern in the hills near a village called Beit Adis and drank from a small spring. These forty days were neither the visions of a starved mind nor the symbolism later recorded as the “⟦Q 136:4.5⟧temptations of Jesus in the wilderness.⟦/Q⟧” He reviewed the whole history of mankind on Urantia, from the days of Andon and Fonta through Adam’s default to the ministry of Melchizedek, and laid plans to serve this world and the other rebellion-isolated spheres.

p136.s5.b0: The following sections present, one by one, the decisions Jesus made in the hills. The common principle is single: not to use superhuman power for himself, to work within natural law and the existing social order, and to surrender everything to the Father’s will.

p136.s5.b2: The first decision had one exception. Since a Personalized Adjuster is a nontime being, it could fully limit the heavenly hosts as to space but not as to time. So, unless the Father ruled otherwise, any supernatural element in Jesus’ ministry pertained wholly to the elimination of time, and to prevent time miracles he had to remain constantly time conscious.
p136.s5.b4: He might use his superhuman power for others, but for himself, never, and he held to this even when mocked on the cross. In light of this decision, the narrator states plainly that he never walked on the water. Prostituting divine gifts for personal aggrandizement was precisely the sin of Lucifer and Caligastia.
p136.s5.b5: Overawing people with miracles would call forth only outward allegiance; it would neither reveal God nor save men. Jesus chose natural, ordinary, difficult, and trying methods, the very procedures his children would later have to follow in extending the kingdom. For those of us who look for shortcuts, his choice is a reminder of the worth of the slow and sure way.
p136.s5.b6: The narrator frankly admits that this inner dialogue held a human element of questioning and near-doubting. If he would do just one unnatural thing, the human mind would know for certain that it was subject to a divine mind. But Jesus judged that it was not the Father’s will for divinity to make that concession to doubt. And because he was incarnate in the mind of a first-century man, his humanity was naturally shaped by the heredity, environment, and education of his time.
p136.s5.b8: He saw that God’s way would not be easy and that the cup of the rest of his human experience might be bitter, but he decided to drink it. Throughout his public ministry he faced the clamor to be fed, the insistence on miracles, and the request to make him king, yet he never departed from the decisions made in the hills. On the last day he gave his pledge to the Adjuster and came down the mountain with his face shining with the glory of spiritual victory.
p136.s6.b0: Paper 136 shows the principles on which Jesus’ public life was built. He held all power, yet he did not use it for himself, for display, or for rule. In doing so he chose a path that would disappoint the Jews’ expectations and lead to his rejection. But that path was the way to reveal the Father.
